opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated pieces of the whole picture, honestly. A lot of the attention in robotics right now goes to pretraining: collect huge amounts of demonstration data, teleoperation, video, simulation, and train a big model that imitates what people do. That gets you surprisingly far. But imitation has a ceiling. The robot only ever sees the good trajectories, the ones where the human did it right. It never really learns what happens when things go slightly wrong, and how to get back.

In the real world, things go slightly wrong all the time. The cup is a few centimeters off, the cloth folds differently, the lighting changes. Small errors compound, and a policy trained purely on clean demonstrations drifts into states it has never seen and doesn't know how to recover from. So the most valuable data, in my view, is exactly the data around failure: the moment the robot makes a mistake, and what the correction looks like.

That's where online correction comes in. You deploy the robot, let it actually act, and when it's about to fail or has just failed, a human steps in. Maybe they nudge it, take over for a few seconds, or just give a signal that this was wrong. That intervention is incredibly information-dense, because it's on the robot's own distribution. It's not someone else's perfect demonstration. It's "here's where you specifically go wrong, and here's how to fix it." A relatively small amount of that kind of data can improve robustness a lot more than another big pile of offline demos.

I also think it changes how we should think about the system as a whole. It stops being "train once, then deploy" and becomes a loop: deploy, observe failures, correct, update, deploy again. That's much closer to how people learn a skill. You don't become a good driver by watching videos of perfect driving. You drive, you make small mistakes, someone corrects you, and you internalize it.

There are real challenges, of course. Human corrections are expensive, so you want the robot to know when it's uncertain and ask for help rather than needing someone watching constantly. The corrections are noisy and inconsistent across people. And doing reinforcement learning on physical hardware is slow and has safety constraints you don't face in simulation. So a lot of the interesting work is in making this loop efficient: better uncertainty estimation, better use of each intervention, and combining real-world correction with simulation and world models so you can amplify a small number of real corrections.

But directionally, I'm quite convinced. Pretraining gives you general capability. Online correction is what turns that into reliability, and reliability is what actually matters if you want robots working in real homes and factories rather than just in demo videos.

fable-5.1.text:
I think correcting a robot's mistakes online is one of the most promising directions, and I'd argue it's where embodied intelligence has to go, because the way we've been training robots is fundamentally different from how humans learn.

Right now most of the field relies on imitation learning. You collect demonstrations, you train a policy, you deploy it, and if it fails, you go back, collect more data, retrain, and deploy again. That loop is slow and expensive, and it never closes. The robot never actually learns from the moment of failure itself. A human doesn't work like that. When a child reaches for a cup and knocks it over, nobody rewrites their brain offline. They adjust right there, in context, and the next attempt is already better.

So online reinforcement with correction is trying to give the robot that same property. The robot acts, it makes a mistake, and a signal arrives, either from a human stepping in or from the environment telling it the outcome, and the policy updates while it's still in the task. The important thing is that the correction is grounded in the robot's own experience, in its own state, with its own embodiment. That's data you simply cannot get from a teleoperation dataset, because demonstrations only show you what success looks like, never how to recover from the specific way this particular robot tends to fail.

There are two hard problems, though. The first is sample efficiency. Real-world interaction is costly and you can't afford millions of trials, so the correction signal has to be dense and informative. That's why I think human-in-the-loop correction is so valuable: a person intervening for two seconds carries far more information than a scalar reward at the end of an episode. The second problem is safety and stability. If you update a policy online, you risk forgetting what it already knew or drifting into unsafe behavior. So the base model has to be strong enough that corrections are small adjustments on top of a good prior, not a rescue of a broken policy.

That's really how I see the pieces fitting together. Large-scale pretraining gives you the common sense and the prior. Online correction gives you adaptation to the specific body, the specific environment, the specific user. The first makes the robot general. The second makes it actually useful. Neither one alone gets you to a robot that works in a real home, and I think the teams that figure out how to make that online loop cheap, safe, and continuous will be the ones who get there first.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very useful feedback loop. When a robot makes a mistake, you have an opportunity to teach it something that may not have been covered in its training data. You can correct the action, let it try again, and use that feedback to improve its behavior.

But the key is whether it learns something that transfers. If you correct how it picks up one cup, does that help it handle a different cup in a different position? Otherwise, you’re just correcting individual mistakes forever.

So I see online reinforcement as a complement to a strong pretrained model. The model gives the robot a starting point, and interaction helps it adapt. The challenge is making those corrections efficient and making sure that learning from a new correction doesn’t break something it already does well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can be a very useful feedback loop. When a robot makes a mistake, a person can correct it, and that correction gives the robot information about what should have happened in that particular situation. The goal is for it to use that feedback to handle similar situations better in the future.

But a correction is not necessarily a reward signal by itself. You need a way to translate that intervention into learning, and you need to make sure the robot generalizes appropriately. Otherwise, it might fix one specific behavior without understanding when that correction applies.

So I see online correction as a way to keep improving a robot after deployment, with people guiding the learning. Ideally, as the robot becomes more capable, the amount of intervention it needs goes down.
